name: Containerized Microservices Architecture
description: Design a production-ready containerized microservices architecture on AWS using ECS/Fargate with service discovery, API management, and asynchronous messaging.
user_problem: Design a containerized microservices architecture on AWS with the following requirements: (1) Container orchestration with serverless compute that eliminates server management, (2) API management for external and inter-service communication, (3) Service discovery for dynamic microservice registration and resolution, (4) Asynchronous messaging between services using queues and pub/sub, (5) Multiple database options including relational, NoSQL, and in-memory caching, (6) Centralized logging, distributed tracing, and monitoring, (7) Container image registry and CI/CD pipeline support, (8) Proper network isolation and load balancing.

reference_architecture.full_text:
A microservices architecture builds an application as independent components that run each application process as a service. These services communicate via well-defined interfaces using lightweight APIs. Services are built for business capabilities and each service performs a single function. Because they are independently run, each service can be updated, deployed, and scaled to meet demand for specific functions of an application. With monolithic architectures, all processes are tightly coupled and run as a single service, meaning if one process experiences a spike in demand, the entire architecture must be scaled. Adding or improving features becomes more complex as the code base grows, limiting experimentation. Monolithic architectures also add risk for application availability because many dependent and tightly coupled processes increase the impact of a single process failure. Microservices solve these challenges through autonomy (each component can be developed, deployed, operated, and scaled independently), specialization (each service focuses on solving a specific problem), flexible scaling (each service can be independently scaled to meet demand), easy deployment (continuous integration and continuous delivery for rapid iteration), technological freedom (teams can choose the best tool for each job), reusable code (functions can be used as building blocks for other features), and resilience (service independence increases resistance to failure).

Container Orchestration and Compute Layer: Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) provides a highly scalable, high-performance container management service that supports Docker containers and allows you to easily run applications on a managed cluster of Amazon EC2 instances or with AWS Fargate. ECS handles cluster management, container scheduling, and service auto-scaling. It supports both EC2 launch type (for full control over instance types and placement) and Fargate launch type (for serverless container execution). AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine that works with both Amazon ECS and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS), eliminating the need to provision and manage servers so developers can focus on building applications. Fargate automatically provisions compute resources based on container CPU and memory requirements. Each Fargate task runs in its own kernel-level isolated environment, providing strong workload isolation. Fargate supports both Linux and Windows containers and integrates with ECS task definitions for resource specification, environment variables, secrets management through AWS Secrets Manager, and logging configuration. ECS Service Auto Scaling automatically adjusts the desired count of tasks in a service based on CloudWatch metrics such as CPU utilization, memory utilization, or custom application metrics. Target tracking scaling policies maintain a target value for a specific metric, while step scaling policies adjust capacity based on alarm thresholds.

API Management Layer: Amazon API Gateway offers a comprehensive platform for API management. It enables creation, publication, maintenance, monitoring, and security of REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at any scale. API Gateway processes hundreds of thousands of concurrent API calls and handles traffic management (throttling and rate limiting), authorization and access control (IAM, Cognito, Lambda authorizers), request/response transformation, monitoring (CloudWatch integration), and API version management (stages and canary deployments). API Gateway supports multiple backend integrations including Lambda, HTTP endpoints, and private resources in VPCs. API Gateway usage plans and API keys enable third-party developer access control and monetization. API Gateway can also serve as the public entry point that routes external traffic to the internal Application Load Balancer, which then distributes to ECS services.

Service Discovery and Networking: AWS Cloud Map provides service discovery for all cloud resources, allowing you to define custom names for application resources and maintaining the updated location of these dynamically changing resources. Cloud Map integrates natively with ECS, automatically registering and deregistering container instances as tasks start and stop. Services can discover each other using DNS queries or the Cloud Map API, enabling dynamic routing without hardcoded endpoint configurations. Application Load Balancer (ALB) provides advanced request routing at the application layer (Layer 7) targeted at the delivery of modern microservices and container architectures. ALB supports path-based routing, host-based routing, HTTP header-based routing, and query string-based routing—allowing a single load balancer to route to multiple microservices. ALB performs health checks on registered targets and only routes traffic to healthy instances. ALB integrates with ECS for dynamic port mapping, enabling multiple containers on the same host to be registered with different target groups. Network Load Balancer (NLB) offers high-performance load balancing at the network connection layer (Layer 4), handling millions of requests per second while maintaining ultra-low latencies. NLB preserves the source IP address and provides static IP addresses for each Availability Zone. NLB is ideal for TCP/UDP protocols and extreme performance requirements. Amazon Route 53 provides highly available and scalable cloud DNS with IP health checks and service discovery for microservices, enabling weighted routing, latency-based routing, and geographic routing for multi-Region deployments. Amazon VPC provides network isolation for microservices. Each microservice can be deployed in private subnets with security groups controlling inbound and outbound traffic. VPC endpoints enable private connectivity to AWS services without traversing the public internet. AWS PrivateLink enables private connectivity between VPCs and services.

Asynchronous Messaging Layer: Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a fully managed message queuing service that enables you to decouple and scale microservices, distributed systems, and serverless applications. SQS supports standard queues for maximum throughput, at-least-once delivery, and best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues for exactly-once processing and strict message ordering. SQS dead-letter queues capture messages that fail processing after a configurable number of retries. SQS supports long polling to reduce empty responses and lower costs. Messages can be up to 256 KB, and the Extended Client Library supports messages up to 2 GB using S3. Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) is a fully managed pub/sub messaging service for both application-to-application (A2A) and application-to-person (A2P) communication. SNS enables high-throughput, push-based, many-to-many messaging between distributed systems, enabling fanout patterns where a single event is pushed to multiple subscribers. SNS supports multiple subscription protocols including SQS, Lambda, HTTP/HTTPS, email, SMS, and mobile push. SNS message filtering allows subscribers to receive only a subset of messages based on filter policies applied to message attributes. SNS FIFO topics work with SQS FIFO queues for strictly ordered messaging.

Data Storage Layer: Amazon DynamoDB offers a fully managed, fast, and flexible NoSQL database service for all applications that need consistent, single-digit millisecond latency at any scale. DynamoDB supports both key-value and document data models. It provides automatic scaling with on-demand capacity mode, global tables for multi-Region replication, and DynamoDB Streams for change data capture. Amazon RDS provides easy setup, operation, and scaling of relational databases in the cloud. RDS supports six database engines: Amazon Aurora, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, and Microsoft SQL Server. RDS handles database administration tasks including provisioning, patching, backup, recovery, fail detection, and repair. Multi-AZ deployments provide high availability with automatic failover. Read replicas improve performance for read-heavy workloads. Amazon Aurora combines the speed and reliability of high-end commercial databases with the simplicity and cost-effectiveness of open-source databases. Aurora delivers up to 5x the throughput of standard MySQL and 3x the throughput of standard PostgreSQL. Aurora supports up to 15 read replicas with sub-10ms replica lag, automatic storage scaling up to 128 TB, and continuous backup to S3. Aurora Serverless v2 automatically adjusts capacity based on application demand. Amazon ElastiCache improves service performance by allowing you to retrieve information from fast, managed, in-memory caches, instead of relying entirely on slower disk-based databases. ElastiCache supports Redis and Memcached engines. Redis provides advanced data structures, pub/sub messaging, Lua scripting, and persistence. ElastiCache provides sub-millisecond latency for caching frequently accessed data, session storage, and real-time analytics.

Container Registry and CI/CD: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) serves as a fully managed Docker container registry for storing, managing, and deploying container images. ECR is integrated with ECS, simplifying the development-to-production workflow. ECR supports image vulnerability scanning via Amazon Inspector, image tag immutability for deployment integrity, and lifecycle policies for automated cleanup of unused images. ECR images are encrypted at rest using AWS KMS. Cross-Region and cross-account replication enables multi-Region and multi-account deployments. AWS CodePipeline, AWS CodeBuild, and AWS CodeDeploy provide a complete CI/CD pipeline. CodePipeline orchestrates build, test, and deployment stages; CodeBuild compiles source code, runs tests, and builds container images; CodeDeploy automates application deployments to ECS with blue/green and rolling update strategies.

Observability Layer: AWS X-Ray provides end-to-end visibility into requests as they travel through the application with a map of underlying components. X-Ray traces follow requests across ECS services, Lambda functions, API Gateway, DynamoDB, SQS, and SNS—identifying latency bottlenecks, errors, and service dependencies. X-Ray service maps provide a real-time topological view of the microservices architecture. Amazon CloudWatch collects and tracks metrics, collects and monitors log files, and sets alarms. CloudWatch Container Insights provides detailed container-level metrics for ECS including CPU, memory, network, and disk utilization per task and service. CloudWatch Logs aggregates application logs from all container instances using the awslogs log driver. CloudWatch ServiceLens combines CloudWatch metrics, logs, traces (X-Ray), and health information for a unified observability experience. CloudWatch Alarms trigger notifications via SNS when operational thresholds are breached. AWS CloudTrail provides continuous monitoring and audit logging of all API calls and account activity across the infrastructure.

Security: AWS IAM provides fine-grained access control with task execution roles and task roles for ECS. Task execution roles grant ECS the permissions to pull container images from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch. Task roles grant containers permissions to access AWS services like DynamoDB, SQS, and S3. AWS Secrets Manager stores and rotates database credentials, API keys, and other secrets that containers retrieve at runtime. Security groups provide instance-level network firewalling. VPC endpoints ensure private connectivity to ECR, S3, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, and CloudWatch without internet access. AWS WAF attached to ALB protects against common web exploits.

The end-to-end data flow is as follows: External clients send requests to Amazon API Gateway or the Application Load Balancer. API Gateway authenticates and throttles requests, then routes to backend ECS services. The ALB performs Layer 7 routing based on path or host headers, distributing requests to the appropriate ECS service target groups. Each microservice runs as a set of Fargate tasks, auto-scaling independently based on demand. Services discover each other via Cloud Map DNS lookups. Synchronous inter-service calls go through the internal NLB or ALB. Asynchronous communication uses SQS for point-to-point and SNS for pub/sub fanout patterns. Each service has its own datastore: DynamoDB for NoSQL, Aurora/RDS for relational, ElastiCache for caching. All requests are traced by X-Ray, metrics and logs flow to CloudWatch, and API calls are recorded by CloudTrail.
